Milvus does not expose a change stream through its gRPC API. Instead, Milvus publishes every write to an internal message queue (MQ) channel before it persists the write. The Debezium Milvus connector reads that channel directly, which means that it connects to three parts of a Milvus deployment: the MQ backend, the etcd cluster that stores channel checkpoints, and the Milvus gRPC endpoint.

The first time that the connector connects to a Milvus cluster, it reads a consistent snapshot of the collections that it is configured to capture. The snapshot is anchored to the channel checkpoint that Milvus records in etcd, so that no change is lost or duplicated when the connector transitions from the snapshot to streaming. After the snapshot completes, the connector begins to emit change events for inserts and deletes that Milvus commits to the captured collections. By default, change events for a particular collection go to a Kafka topic that is named after the collection. Applications and services can then consume change event records from these topics.

The Debezium connector for Milvus is currently in the Incubating stage of development. You are encouraged to explore and test the connector, but it is not yet recommended for production use. The format of emitted messages may change, specific features may not be implemented, and it is expected to evolve before it is production-ready.

Milvus organizes its internal change stream around two kinds of channels: physical channels (pchannels) and virtual channels (vchannels). A pchannel is a real topic on the message queue backend; in a Kafka-backed deployment, each pchannel is an ordinary Kafka topic that Milvus writes all data manipulation operations into. A vchannel is a logical stream within a pchannel that carries the changes of a single collection shard. Milvus does not create a separate topic for each vchannel. Instead, it multiplexes several vchannels onto one pchannel and tags each message with the name of the vchannel that it belongs to, much as multiple logical event streams can share a single Kafka topic and be separated again by a message attribute. When a collection is created, Milvus assigns each of its shards a vchannel, and maps that vchannel onto one of the cluster’s pchannels. Alongside insert and delete messages, Milvus periodically publishes
messages on each vchannel; a timetick acts like a watermark that advances the vchannel’s logical clock and tells consumers that no earlier-timestamped changes will arrive on that channel.

Milvus tracks how far it has consumed and persisted each channel by recording a per-channel

timestamp and the MQ offset that corresponds to it. Every operation at or before the checkpoint is durably stored in Milvus, which is what makes the checkpoint a safe anchor for the snapshot and a safe position from which to resume streaming. Because the Milvus API does not expose checkpoint data, the connector requires direct access to the etcd cluster that backs Milvus.

During the snapshot, the connector uses the API to list collections, read their schemas, and query rows. During streaming, the connector uses the API to resolve the schema of a collection that it has not yet observed in an insert event.

Milvus assigns every operation a timestamp from a Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC), which the Milvus documentation refers to as a TSO (timestamp oracle). The high 46 bits of a TSO encode the number of milliseconds that elapsed since the UNIX epoch, and the low 18 bits encode a logical counter that orders operations that occur within the same millisecond. The connector preserves this value in the
block of every event, and uses it to order events across vchannels.
To optimally configure and run a Debezium Milvus connector, it is helpful to understand how the connector performs snapshots, orders events, and names topics.

If the etcd checkpoint does not exist, for example, because the Milvus cluster has not yet written to the pchannel, the snapshot completes immediately without emitting rows, and the streaming phase falls back to the latest position in the MQ.
If the connector fails after the snapshot begins but before it completes, the connector starts a new snapshot after it restarts.

The connector does not take a separate schema snapshot. Milvus collection schemas are resolved dynamically, either from the Milvus metadata API during the snapshot, or from the first insert event that the connector observes during streaming.
The connector performs a snapshot when no offsets exist, and then streams changes. This is the default.
The connector never performs a snapshot. It begins streaming from the position that its stored offsets specify, or from the latest position in the MQ if no offsets exist.
The connector performs a snapshot if no offsets exist, or if the stored offsets refer to a position that is no longer available in the MQ.
The Milvus connector does not support incremental snapshots, ad hoc snapshots, or blocking snapshots.

After the snapshot completes, the connector seeks its MQ consumer to the offset that the etcd checkpoint recorded, and enters the streaming loop. For each iteration, the connector completes the following steps:
Polls a batch of raw messages from the pchannel topic.

Deserializes each message. Depending on its version, a Milvus cluster uses one of two wire formats for its MQ payloads: a msgpack batch envelope, or a single protobuf message per record. By default the

, which causes the connector to probe the channel and detect the format that the cluster uses. The connector expects the format to stay consistent on the same channel; if it changes, the connector reports an error.

Buffers the deserialized events. Because several vchannels share the pchannel, and each vchannel advances its own timetick independently, events can arrive on the topic in a different order than the order they were committed. The connector must hold each event in a buffer, the
, until it can guarantee that no earlier operation is still inflight.
Flushes events whose TSO is behind the

, which is the minimum timetick across all active vchannels. Because no vchannel can subsequently produce an event with a lower TSO, the flushed events are guaranteed to be complete and are released in strict TSO order.

Dispatches the flushed events to the Debezium event pipeline, and only afterwards advances the connector offsets with the new MQ position and vchannel watermarks. Updating offsets after dispatch ensures that the connector never commits an offset for an event that it did not emit.
If a vchannel stops advancing its timetick for longer than the interval that the

property specifies, the connector logs a warning and force-flushes the buffered events rather than stalling indefinitely. To bound memory use, the ordering engine applies backpressure when the buffer exceeds the limits that the

After a restart, the connector initializes the ordering engine with the vchannel watermarks that it stored in its offsets, so that streaming resumes without waiting for a fresh timetick from every vchannel.

The Debezium Milvus connector generates a data change event for each row-level insert and delete operation. Each event contains a key and a value. The structure of the key and value depends on the collection that was changed.

Milvus implements upserts as a delete followed by an insert, and the connector emits that pair of operations as it observes them on the channel; therefore, it emits no update (
) event. A downstream consumer will observe an upsert as a delete event, followed by a tombstone unless
, and finally the insert with the same key, rather than a single update event.

Collection creation and removal are tracked internally, so that the connector can order events correctly, but they are not emitted as schema change events. The connector does not produce a schema change topic.
